rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāʾif denotes a visitation from Satan, perhaps experienced as a dream or apparition, and so describes temptation.
rows.anchor: which is the lexical meaning of ṭāʾif (Z), translated here as “visitation.”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some take Satan's visitation as an impulse toward anger.
rows.anchor: Some consider a visitation from Satan to refer here to the impulse toward anger (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Others take it as any Satanic whispering that tempts a person toward moral or intellectual lapse.
rows.anchor: or to any Satanic insinuation (“whispering”; see 114:4c) that tempts one toward a moral or intellectual lapse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reverent remember God, especially His commands and threat of punishment, and return to obedience.
rows.anchor: they remember God, and in particular they remember the commands of God and the threat of His punishment—and so return to obedience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tadhakkarū can mean to reflect or take heed as well as to remember.
rows.anchor: which can also mean to“reflect” or “take heed.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After remembering, the reverent regain sound judgment and guidance and return to what is right and commanded by God.
rows.anchor: they are restored to sound judgment and guidance (Ṭs) and return to what is right and what God has commanded

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says that remembering God whenever tempted is the reverent person's regular habit.
rows.anchor: According to al-Zamakhsharī“remembering” God in this way whenever one is tempted is the regular habit of the reverent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The near-synonymous commands to hearken and listen emphasize careful attention to the Quran's sacred recitation.
rows.anchor: employing two words that are nearly synonyms, serves to emphasize the care with which one should listen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Careful listening entails understanding the Quran's meaning, reflecting on its teachings, and acting on its prescriptions.
rows.anchor: paying full attention in order to understand its meaning as well as reflecting upon its teachings (Aj, Ṭ) and acting according to its prescriptions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anṣitū connotes listening silently.
rows.anchor: Listen translates anṣitū, which connotes listening silently

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say silence was particularly important when the Prophet recited the Quran.
rows.anchor: some indicate was particularly important when the Prophet was reciting the Quran (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In communal prayer, those behind the imam must silently attend to his Quranic recitation, neither talking nor reciting aloud themselves.
rows.anchor: requiring all those praying behind the imam to be silent and listen attentively to the Quranic passages

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators apply attentive listening whenever one hears the Quran recited, in any context.
rows.anchor: Some commentators assert that the command to listen attentively to the recited Quran applies to any context in which one hears it

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Silent, receptive listening is seen as cultivating pure servitude to God or entry into His Presence as the ultimate Speaker behind the recitation.
rows.anchor: Listening silently and with pure receptivity to the recited Quran is considered by some as a means of developing the quality of pure servitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the preceding verse calls the Quran a mercy, attentive hearing of its recitation is a means of receiving mercy.
rows.anchor: Since the Quran is described in v. 203 as a mercy, one should hearken to its recited words so one may receive mercy

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah says mercy is the closest thing to the person listening to the Quran.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAjībah states that “mercy is the closest thing to the one listening to the Quran.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to remember the Lord is addressed to the Prophet but applies to everyone.
rows.anchor: The command to remember thy Lord is addressed to the Prophet, but applies to all people (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remembrance likely includes both verbal invocation of God and remembrance in the heart.
rows.anchor: It likely refers to both the invocation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembrance may take the form of Quran recitation, praise and glorification, or the testimony to God's Oneness.
rows.anchor: This “remembrance” may also take the form of reciting the Quran or uttering words of praise and glorification for God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read after the previous verse, the command may mean remembering God while hearing Quran recitation.
rows.anchor: Read in connection with the previous verse, remember thy Lord may be an injunction to remember God when one hears the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God within one's soul can also mean remembering Him within oneself.
rows.anchor: To remember God within thy soul may also mean to remember Him “within thyself,”

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī connects the verse to a sacred hadith: when a servant remembers God privately or in an assembly, God remembers him correspondingly, in a nobler assembly in the latter case.
rows.anchor: al-Ṭabarīconnects this verse with a famous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is a major basis for dhikr, especially in Sufism, as a means of unveiling and deeper understanding of God.
rows.anchor: The present verse is one of the most important in suggesting the spiritual importance of dhikr (remembrance or invocation)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr allows recognition that God is near and witnesses one's thoughts and deeds, and can lead to experiencing His Presence.
rows.anchor: as a means of experiencing His Presence and one’s immersion “in the ocean of Divinity.”

rows.speaker: a ḥadīth
rows.claim: A hadith says everything on earth is accursed except remembrance of God.
rows.anchor: According to a ḥadīth, “All that is on the earth is accursed save the remembrance of God.”

words: تَضَرُّعًۭا وَخِيفَةًۭ وَدُونَ ٱلْجَهْرِ مِنَ ٱلْقَوْلِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humble, quiet remembrance resembles commands to supplicate humbly and secretly and guides Sufi dhikr practice.
rows.anchor: The command to remember God humbly and in awe, being not loud of voice, is similar to the command to call upon Him humbly and in secret

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lowering the voice is also enjoined in supplication, speech before the Prophet, and general conduct; the Quran likens the vilest voices to donkeys.
rows.anchor: Lowering one’s voice is also enjoined during supplicatory prayer (17:110), when speaking in the presence of the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quiet prayer signals sincerity rather than seeking to be seen and helps reflection and recollection.
rows.anchor: To pray quietly reflects sincerity in one’s prayer (Aj, R, Z), indicating that one is not praying to be seen of men

rows.speaker: the Companions
rows.claim: When Companions asked whether God was near enough for whispers or far enough to require shouts, 2:186 was revealed affirming His nearness and response to callers.
rows.anchor: The Prophet was once asked by some Companions whether God was near, so that they should whisper to Him, or far away, so that they should shout

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says invocation should be audible to oneself, not wholly silent: bodily hearing stirs imagination and soul, strengthening the spiritual heart as body, soul, and spirit reinforce one another.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī explains that the invocation or remembrance enjoined here should be done not silently, but in a voice low enough that it can be heard only by oneself

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The quiet-voice command might be taken to prohibit loud communal Sufi dhikr.
rows.anchor: some might consider this verse as prohibiting the loud, communal dhikr practiced by Sufi groups.

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah rejects using the verse to ban loud communal dhikr: it was revealed in Mecca amid circumspect worship, while the Prophet and Companions later held public mosque dhikr in Medina.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAjībah, however, rejects this interpretation, noting that this verse was revealed in Makkah, when the believers had to be circumspect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Morning and evening are especially suited times for remembrance, supplication, and praise; they may also represent remembrance at all times.
rows.anchor: The morning and the evening are mentioned here and elsewhere as times particularly suited to remembering, supplicating, or praising God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Morning and evening symbolize transitions between light and dark and sleep and waking, suggesting death and resurrection.
rows.anchor: each being a time of transition between light and darkness, sleeping and waking, and thus suggestive of death and resurrection (Aj, R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What gives life may be the truth or the Quran, which gives life to the heart and brings commands leading to everlasting life in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: That which will give you life is the truth, or the Quran itself (Ṭ), meaning something that gives life to the heart

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The call that gives life may also be the call to fight in God's way, since dying in that cause leads to everlasting felicity.
rows.anchor: This verse could also mean that one should respond to the call to fighting in the way of God, since death in the way of God would lead to everlasting felicity

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God comes between a disbeliever and faith, or between a believer and disbelief.
rows.anchor: interpreted to mean that He comes between a disbeliever and faith, or between a believer and disbelief (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that nothing, including the innermost dimensions of a person, is hidden from God, as in the image of His nearness to the jugular vein.
rows.anchor: or that nothing is hidden from God, even the innermost dimensions of one’s being (Ṭ). In this sense it resembles the statement in 50:16

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The phrase can mean God has power to change hearts, as when He changed the Badr participants' fear into security.
rows.anchor: It can also mean that God has the power to change hearts, as when He changed the fear in the hearts of the participants of the Battle of Badr into a sense of security

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gathering of all creatures to God recurs throughout the Quran and connects with its repeated teaching that all things return to Him.
rows.anchor: The notion of being gathered unto God is mentioned throughout the Quran (e.g., 2:203; 3:158; 5:96; 6:38; 23:79; 58:9; 67:24)

words: بِٱلْعُدْوَةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَهُم بِٱلْعُدْوَةِ ٱلْقُصْوَىٰ وَٱلرَّكْبُ أَسْفَلَ مِنكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Badr the two armies stood on opposite sides of a valley, with Abū Sufyān's caravan below them toward the sea.
rows.anchor: the two armies were on two sides of a valley with the caravan of Abū Sufyān below them in the direction of the sea (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had they arranged to meet, the Muslims would not have agreed to face such a superior army had they known its strength.
rows.anchor: the Muslims would not have agreed to go out to meet such a superior army in battle if they had prior knowledge of it (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The matter God brought about was destined and necessarily had to come to pass.
rows.anchor: The battle is described as a matter that was to be done, meaning that it necessarily had to come to pass (R).

words: لِّيَهْلِكَ مَنْ هَلَكَ عَنۢ بَيِّنَةٍۢ وَيَحْيَىٰ مَنْ حَىَّ عَنۢ بَيِّنَةٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clear-proof wording echoes the separation of bad from good in 8:37 and the Badr Day of Discrimination, which exposed truth and falsehood through the battle.
rows.anchor: echoes the separation of the bad from the good in v. 37 and the idea that the Battle of Badr was a Day of Discrimination

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some interpret the clear proof as the rain before battle, which reversed the Makkan advantage of firmer ground over the Muslims' soft ground.
rows.anchor: A clear proof is interpreted by some to refer to the rain that came just before the battle and miraculously reversed the advantage the Makkans had

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others understand the clear proof more broadly as the smaller, poorly equipped Muslim army's victory over Quraysh, three times its size and well armed.
rows.anchor: others see it more broadly as the fact that the smaller and poorly equipped army of the Muslims defeated the well-armed contingent of Quraysh

rows.speaker: the most common account
rows.claim: The verse concerns men who stayed behind from Tabūk, repented, tied themselves to mosque walls, and vowed to abstain from food and drink until pardoned.
rows.anchor: According to the most common account, this verse was revealed in connection with several men who had remained behind from the Tabūk campaign

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some take the righteous deeds mixed with sins to include the men's earlier participation in battles alongside the Prophet.
rows.anchor: could refer to the fact that some of these men had previously

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some understand God's expression may He relent as conveying necessity because it comes from God.
rows.anchor: Some consider that, coming from God, it may be implies a necessity (R, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speech on the Last Day only by God's permission is also stated in 78:38 and 20:108, with 36:65 as a comparison.
rows.anchor: That none will be allowed to speak on the Last Day except with God’s Permission is also related in 78:38

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wretched and felicitous refer respectively to the damned and the saved.
rows.anchor: The terms the wretched and the felicitous refer to the damned and the saved, respectively

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These are common terms for the two groups in Islamic writings and have received extensive attention, especially in Sufi literature.
rows.anchor: these are among the more commonly used terms for these two groups in Islamic texts, and much has been written, especially in Sufi literature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell's groaning and wailing describe heavy breathing, ceaseless weeping, and extreme pain, regret, and incurable grief.
rows.anchor: which means that they will be breathing heavily, weeping ceaselessly, and experiencing an extreme state of pain, regret, and incurable grief (R).

rows.speaker: al-Bayḍāwī
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī says the heavens and earth enduring refers to the Afterlife's basic topographic setting, not serial time or physical-world time; 14:48 depicts the earth and heavens changed on that Day.
rows.anchor: Bayḍāwī argues that the period in Hell described as for so long as

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden's unending gift means that it will never cease.
rows.anchor: with the added nuance that it is a gift unfailing, which is interpreted to mean that the Garden will never cease (Kl).

rows.speaker: Ibn Taymiyyah
rows.claim: Ibn Taymiyyah reads verse 107's wording as clear evidence that Hell itself will eventually cease to exist.
rows.anchor: According to the seventh/thirteenth-century Damascene theologian and jurist Ibn Taymiyyah (d. 728/1328), the wording in v. 107 is a clear indication that Hell itself will one day cease to exist

rows.speaker: many Islamic authorities, especially Sufis
rows.claim: Many other authorities, especially Sufis, also assert that Hell will eventually cease or freeze over.
rows.anchor: The thesis that Hell would one day cease to exist or“freeze over” is also asserted by many other Islamic authorities, especially Sufis.

words: فَلَوْلَا كَانَ مِنَ ٱلْقُرُونِ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ
rows.speaker: al-Ṭūsī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭūsī says the question is meant to produce wonder that past communities had only a few righteous people, while the rest were disbelievers deserving punishment.
rows.anchor: The Shiite Quran commentator al-Ṭūsī observes that, in asking the question in v. 116, God intends to produce wonder and amazement

rows.speaker: al-Ṭūsī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭūsī's reading highlights that only a few in earlier communities were righteous, while most were disbelievers who merited punishment.
rows.anchor: that in past communities there were only a few who were righteous while the rest were disbelievers who deserved punishment.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read 11:117 to mean God would not destroy a people merely for disbelief if their worldly dealings and conduct were fair and honest.
rows.anchor: Some interpret v. 117 to mean that God would not destroy a people just because they were disbelievers if their worldly transactions and conduct could be characterized as fair and honest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The peoples of Noah, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, and Shuʿayb were destroyed utterly because they harmed their own souls, other people, and other creatures.
rows.anchor: the peoples of Noah, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, and Shuʿayb were destroyed utterly when God characterized them as harming not only their own souls, but also other human beings and other creatures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows whether each female's offspring will be male or female, sound or deficient, and tall or short.
rows.anchor: whether it will be a male or female, sound or deficient, tall or short (R);

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More importantly, God knows each soul's inner workings before it is born.
rows.anchor: and, more important, He knows the inner workings of each soul before it is born

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wombs diminishing or increasing refers to the length of each pregnancy's gestation.
rows.anchor: How wombs diminish and how they increase refers to the length of the gestation period in each womb (JJ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God as Knower of the Unseen and the seen is also described in 6:59 and 59:22.
rows.anchor: For God as Knower of the Unseen and the seen, see 6:59; 59:22c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording about measure recalls 54:49, which says all things were created according to a measure; the theological significance of qadar is discussed there.
rows.anchor: evokes the use of measure in 54:49: Truly We have created everything according to a measure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following 13:9's account of God's all-encompassing knowledge, this verse means He knows everyone's actions whatever their situation.
rows.anchor: Following directly upon v. 9, which speaks of God’s all-encompassing Knowledge (Bḍ), this verse is understood to mean that no matter what one’s condition is, God is fully aware of one’s actions

words: مَنْ أَسَرَّ ٱلْقَوْلَ وَمَن جَهَرَ بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awareness of God's knowledge should produce vigilance in action and constant, intense scrutiny of one's thoughts and heart.
rows.anchor: This fact is meant to engender not only vigilance in one’s actions

rows.speaker: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb
rows.claim: The second Caliph ʿUmar is reported to have urged people to take themselves to account before they are held to account.
rows.anchor: As the second CaliphʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The separated letters are discussed at 2:1.
rows.anchor: For the separated letters, see 2:1c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book refers to the Quran.
rows.anchor: A Book refers to the Quran (Bg, My, Ṭ; cf. 13:1).

words: لِتُخْرِجَ ٱلنَّاسَ مِنَ ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ إِلَى ٱلنُّورِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By calling people to the Quran, the Prophet leads them from disbelief, ignorance, and doubt to guidance, knowledge, and certainty.
rows.anchor: By means of calling people to the Quran (Q), the Prophet brings human beings out of darkness into light, that is, from the darkness of disbelief, ignorance, and doubt

words: لِتُخْرِجَ ٱلنَّاسَ مِنَ ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ إِلَى ٱلنُّورِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A similar image of bringing people from darkness to light appears at 14:5 and 65:11; elsewhere God is the subject of this image.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere in the Quran God is the subject of similar phrases in which He is said to bring forth mankind out of darkness into light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By their Lord's leave refers to God's kindness in bestowing grace and granting people success in guidance.
rows.anchor: By the leave of their Lord refers to God’s Kindness in bestowing grace upon people and granting them success in being guided out of darkness into light

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The path may mean the light mentioned here or Islam itself.
rows.anchor: The path can refer to being led to the light mentioned in this verse (Aj), or to Islam itself (AF).

rows.speaker: al-Qummī
rows.claim: Al-Qummī interprets the path as the leadership of the Twelve Imams.
rows.anchor: Qummī, the path refers to the leadership of the Twelve Imams.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mighty signifies God's perfect Power, while Praised means that He deserves praise in all that He does.
rows.anchor: The name Mighty refers to the perfection of God’s Power, whereas the name Praised means that God is deserving of praise in all that He does (R)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: One account says that after Hagar bore Ishmael, jealous Sarah prompted Abraham to take Hagar and Ishmael from Syria to Mecca; therefore the land is Mecca.
rows.anchor: It is said that when Hagar gave birth to Ishmael, Sarah became jealous of her; so Abraham took Hagar and Ishmael from Syria to Makkah.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some identify 29:67 as the answer to Abraham's prayer that Mecca be made secure.
rows.anchor: Some commentators see the answer to Abraham’s prayer that Makkah be made secure in the wording of 29:67

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks that he and his children be kept entirely distant from idol worship.
rows.anchor: When Abraham says, Keep me and my children from worshipping idols, he is saying, “Make me and my children totally distant from idol worship” (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another aspect of Abraham's prayer at Mecca is discussed in the commentary on 2:126–129.
rows.anchor: For another aspect of Abraham’s prayer at Makkah, see commentary on 2:126–29.
